[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
### 1.1 Viewing the World at Different Scales The world puts on different faces for observers using different scales in the measurement of space and time. The everyday, macroscopic world, as perceived on the scale of meters and seconds, looks very different from that of the atomic, microscopic world, which is seen on scales smaller by some ten orders of magnitude. Different still is the submicroscopic ealm of quarks, which is revealed only when the scale shrinks further by another ten orders of magnitude. With an expanding scale in the opposite direction, one enters the regime of astronomy, and ultimately cosmology. These different pictures arise from different ways of organizing data, while the basic laws of physics remain the same. The physical laws at the smallest accessible length scale are the most "fundamental," but they are of little use on a larger scale, where we must deal with different physical variables. A complete knowledge of quarks tells us nothing about the structure of nuclei, unless we can define nuclear variables in terms of quarks, and obtain their equations of motion from those for quarks. Needless to say, we are unable to do this in detail, although we can see how this could be done in principle.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
Therefore, each regime of scales has to be described phenomenologically, in terms of variables and laws observable in that regime. For example, an atom is described in terms of electrons and nuclei without reference to quarks. The subnuclear world enters the equations only implicitly, through such parameters as the mass ratio of electron to proton, which we take from experiments in the atomic regime. Similarly, in the macroscopic domain, where atoms are too small to be visible, we describe matter in terms of phenomenological variables such as pressure and temperature.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
The atomic structure of matter enters the picture implicitly, in terms of properties such as density and heat capacity, which can be measured by macroscopic instruments. This book is concerned mainly with statistical methods, which provide a bridge between the microscopic and the macroscopic world.

We begin our study with thermodynamics, because it is a highly successful phenomenological theory, which identifies the correct macroscopic variables to use, and serves as a guidepost for statistical mechanics.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
### 1.2 Thermodynamics From experience, we know that a macroscopic body generally settles down, or "relaxes" to a stationary state after a short time. We call this a state of thermal equilibrium When the external condition is changed, the existing equilibrium state will change, and, after a relatively short relaxation time, settles down to another equilibrium state. Thus, a macroscopic body spends most of the time in some state of equilibrium, punctuated by almost sudden transitions. In our study of macroscopic phenomena, we divide the subject roughly under the following headings: - Thermodynamics is a phenomenological theory of equilibrium states and transitions among them. - Statistical mechanics is concerned with deducing the thermodynamic properties of a macroscopic system from its microscopic structure. - Kinetic theory aims at a microscopic description of the transition process between equilibrium states. As a rule, properties of a macroscopic system can be classified as either extensive or intensive:

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
- Extensive quantities are proportional to the amount of stuff present. - Intensive quantities are independent of the amount of stuff present. Generally, there are only these two categories, because we can neglect surface effects.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
A macroscopic body is typically of size $L \sim 1 \mathrm{~m}$, while the range of atomic forces is of order $r_{0} \sim 10^{-10} \mathrm{~m}$. The macroscopic nature is expressed by the ratio $L / r_{0} \sim 10^{10}$. The surface to volume ratio, rendered dimensionless in terms of the range of atomic forces, is of order $r_{0} / L \sim 10^{-10}$. The extensive property expresses the "saturation property" of atomic forces, that is, an atom can "feel" only as far as the range of the force.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
The intensive property means that atoms in the interior of the body do not feel the presence of the surface. Exceptions arise when one of the following conditions prevail: - The system is small. - There is a nonuniform external potential. - There are long-range interparticle forces, such as the Coulomb repulsion between charges, and the gravitational attraction between mass elements. - The geometry is such that the surface is important.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
These exceptions occur in important physical systems. For example, the volume of a star is a nonlinear function of its mass, due to the long-ranged gravitational interaction. We illustrate the different cases in Figure 1.1.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
![ This diagram depicts examples of particle or system configurations illustrating the concept of extensivity in physical systems, showing how extensive systems maintain proportional scaling when divided, while non-extensive systems do not due to factors like small size, long-range interactions, or irregular shapes.](http://localhost:5001/subjects/065313dc-e010-4cf3-9daf-525801a906a2/images/204ead23-7ec3-4dd2-a9ff-40b5f38aa220/28642244-d175-43cc-88d7-d1a09b8e51d0-03_917_1040_250_383.jpg) Figure 1.1 A body has extensive properties if surface effects can be neglected, so that the energy is proportional to the number of particles. In these pictures, the surface layer is indicated by a heavy line.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
### 1.3 The Thermodynamic Limit We consider a material body consisting of $N$ atoms in volume $V$, in the absence of a nonuniform external potential, to be the idealized limit $$ \begin{aligned} N & \rightarrow \infty \\ V & \rightarrow \infty \\ \frac{N}{V} & =\text { fixed number } \end{aligned}

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
$$ This is called the thermodynamic limit, in which the system becomes translationally invariant. The thermodynamic state is specified by a number of thermodynamic variables, which are assumed to be either extensive (proportional to $N$ ), or intensive (independent of $N$ ). We consider a generic system described by the three variables $P, V, T$, denoting, pressure, volume, and temperature respectively: - The pressure $P$, an intensive quantity, is the force per unit area that the body exerts on a wall, which can be that of the container of the system, or it may be one side of an imaginary surface inside the body. Under equilibrium conditions in the absence of external potentials, the pressure must be uniform throughout

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
the body. It is convenient to measure pressure in terms of the atmospheric pressure at sea level: 1 \mathrm{~atm}=1.013 \times 10^{6} \text { dyne } \mathrm{cm}^{-2}=1.103 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2} - The volume $V$ measures the spatial extent of the body, and is an extensive quantity.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
A solid body maintains its own characteristic density $N / V$. A gas, however, fills the entire volume of its container. - The temperature $T$, an intensive quantity, is measured by some thermometer. It is an indicator of thermal equilibrium.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
Two bodies in contact with each other in equilibrium must have the same temperature. Since the two bodies in question can be different parts of the same body, the temperature of a body in equilibrium must be uniform. The temperature also indicates the energy content of a body, but the notion of energy has yet to be defined, through the first law of thermodynamics. In the thermodynamic limit we must use only intensive quantities, mathematically speaking.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
Instead of $V$ we should use the specific volume $v=V / N$, or the density $n=N / V$. However, it is convenient to regard $V$ as a large but finite number, for this corresponds to the everyday experience of seeing the volume of a macroscopic body expand or contract, while the number of atoms is fixed. There are systems requiring other variables in addition to, or in place of, $P, V, T$. Common examples are the magnetic field and magnetization for a magnetic substance, the strain and stress in elastic solids, or the surface area and the surface tension.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
### 1.4 Thermodynamic Transformations When a body is in thermal equilibrium, the thermodynamic variables are not independent of one another, but are constrained by an equation of state of the form f(P, V, T)=0

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
where the function $f$ is characteristic of the substance. This leaves two independent variables out of the original three. Geometrically we can represent the equation of state by a surface in the state space spanned by $P, V, T$, as shown in Figure 1.2. All equilibrium states must lie on this surface.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
We regard $f$ as a continuous differentiable function, except possibly at special points. A change in the external condition will change the equilibrium state of a system. For example, application of external pressure will cause the volume of a body to decrease. Such a change is called a thermodynamic transformation. The initial and final states are equilibrium states. The system can be considered to remain in equilibrium, if the transformation proceeds sufficiently slowly. In such a case, we say that the transformation is quasi-static. This usually means that the transformation is reversible, in that the system will retrace the transformation in reverse, when the external change

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
![ This diagram depicts a thermodynamic state surface showing the pressure (P), temperature (T), and volume (V) relationship, illustrating reversible and irreversible paths between two states (A and B) on the equation of state surface.](http://localhost:5001/subjects/065313dc-e010-4cf3-9daf-525801a906a2/images/204ead23-7ec3-4dd2-a9ff-40b5f38aa220/28642244-d175-43cc-88d7-d1a09b8e51d0-05_612_692_265_559.jpg) Figure 1.2 The state space in thermodynamics. is reversed. A reversible transformation can be represented by a continuous path on the equation-of-state surface, as illustrated in Figure 1.2. An irreversible transformation, on the other hand, cannot be represented by a path on the equation-of-state space, as indicated by the dashed line in Figure 1.2. In fact, we may not be able to represent it as a path in the state space at all. An example is the sudden removal of a wall in a container of a gas, so that the gas expands into a compartment that was originally vacuous. Although the initial and final states are equilibrium states, the intermediate states do not have uniform $P, V, T$, and hence cannot be represented as points in the state space. In a reversible transformation, we can consider mathematically infinitesimal paths. The mechanical work done by the system over an infinitesimal path is represented by a differential: d W=P d V Along a finite reversible path $A \rightarrow B$, the work done is given by \Delta W=\int_{A}^{B} P d V which depends on the path connecting $A$ to $B$. This is the area underneath the path in a $P V$ diagram. When the path is a closed cycle, the work done in one cycle is the area enclosed, as shown in Figure 1.3. The work done along an irreversible path is generally not $\int P d V$. For example, in the free expansion of a gas into a vacuum, the system does not perform work on any external agent, and so $\Delta W=0$. A uniquely thermodynamic process is heat transfer.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
From the atomic point of view, it represents a transfer of energy in the form of thermal agitation. In thermodynamics, we define heat phenomenologically, as that imparted by a heating element, such as a flame or a heating coil. An amount of heat $\Delta Q$ absorbed by a body causes a rise $\Delta T$ in its temperature given by

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
\Delta Q=C \Delta T ![ This diagram depicts a pressure-volume (P-V) cycle for a thermodynamic process, showing the work done by the system during one complete cycle.](http://localhost:5001/subjects/065313dc-e010-4cf3-9daf-525801a906a2/images/204ead23-7ec3-4dd2-a9ff-40b5f38aa220/28642244-d175-43cc-88d7-d1a09b8e51d0-06_562_564_248_613.jpg) Figure 1.3 The work done in a closed cycle of transformations is represented by the area enclosed by the cycle in a $\boldsymbol{P} \boldsymbol{V}$ diagram. where $C$ is the heat capacity of the substance.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
We imagine the limit in which $\Delta Q$ and $\Delta T$ become infinitesimal. The heat capacity is an extensive quantity. The intensive heat capacity per particle $C / N$, per mole $C / n$, or per unit volume $C / V$, is called specific heat. The fact that heat is a form of energy was established experimentally, by observing that one can increase the temperature of a body by $\Delta T$ either by transferring heat to the body or performing work on it. A practical unit for heat is the calorie (cal), originally defined as that amount of heat that will raise the temperature of 1 g of water from 14.5 to $15.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ at sea level. In current usage, it is defined exactly in terms of the joule (J): 1 \mathrm{cal} \equiv 4.184 \mathrm{~J} Another commonly used unit is the British thermal unit (Btu): 1 \mathrm{Btu} \equiv 1055 \mathrm{~J} The heat absorbed by a body depends on the path of the transformation, as is true of the mechanical work done by the body.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
We can speak of the amount of heat absorbed in a process, but the "heat of a body," like the "work of a body," is meaningless. Commonly encountered transformations are the following: - $T=$ constant (isothermal process) - $P=$ constant (isobaric process) - $V=$ constant (constant-volume process)

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
- $\Delta Q=0$ (adiabatic process) We use a subscript to distinguish the different types of paths, as for example $C_{V}$ and $C_{P}$, representing, respectively, the heat capacity at constant volume and constant pressure. The heat capacity is only one of many thermodynamic coefficients

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
that measure the response of the system to an external source. Other examples are \begin{aligned} & \kappa=-\frac{1}{V} \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta P} \quad \text { (compressibility) } \\ & \alpha=\frac{1}{V} \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta T} \quad \text { (coefficient of thermal expansion) } \end{aligned} These coefficients can be obtained from experimental measurements. In principle they can be calculated from atomic properties using statistical mechanics.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
### 1.5 Classic Ideal Gas The simplest thermodynamic system is the classic ideal gas, which is a gas in the limit of low density and high temperature. The equation of state is given by the ideal gas law:

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
P V=N k_{B} T where $T$ is the ideal gas temperature, measured in kelvins ( K ), and k_{B}=1.381 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{erg} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}(\text { Boltzmann's constant }) As we shall see, the second law of thermodynamics implies $T>0$, and the lower bound is called the absolute zero.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
For this reason, $T$ is also called the absolute temperature. The heat capacity of a monatomic ideal gas at constant volume $C_{V}$ has the value C_{V}=\frac{3}{2} N k_{B} These properties of the ideal gas were established experimentally, and can be derived theoretically in statistical mechanics.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
Thermodynamics does not assume the existence of atoms. Instead of the number of atoms $N$, we can use the number of gram moles $n$, which is a chemical property of the substance. The two are related through

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
N k_{B} & =n R \\ R & =8.314 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{erg} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}(\text { gas constant }) The ratio $R / k_{B}$ is Avogadro's number, the number of atoms per mole: A_{0}=\frac{R}{k_{B}}=6.022 \times 10^{23} ![

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
This diagram is a Pressure-Volume (P-V) diagram showing isothermal processes for an ideal gas at three different temperatures (T1 > T2 > T3), illustrating the relationship between pressure and volume along isotherms. It depicts points and transitions between states on these isotherms, indicating changes in pressure and volume at constant temperatures.](http://localhost:5001/subjects/065313dc-e010-4cf3-9daf-525801a906a2/images/204ead23-7ec3-4dd2-a9ff-40b5f38aa220/28642244-d175-43cc-88d7-d1a09b8e51d0-08_705_759_261_526.jpg) Figure 1.4 Isotherms of an ideal gas, and various paths of transformations. Indeed, the atomic picture was a latecomer that gained acceptance only after a long historic struggle (See Section 10.7). The equation of state can be represented graphically in a $P V$ diagram, as shown in Figure 1.4, which displays a family of curves at constant $T$ called isotherms. Indicated on this graph are the reversible paths corresponding to various types of transformations:

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
- $a b$ is isothermal. - $b c$ proceeds at constant volume. - $c d$ is at constant pressure. - de is isothermal. - abcdea is a closed cycle. - $d f$ is nonisothermal. To keep the temperature constant during an isothermal transformation, we keep the system in thermal contact with a body so large that its temperature is not noticeably affected by heat exchange with our system. We call such a body a heat reservoir, or heat bath.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
### 1.6 First Law of Thermodynamics The first law expresses the conservation of energy by including heat as a form of energy. It asserts that there exists a function of the state, internal energy $U$, whose change in any thermodynamic transformation is given by \Delta U=\Delta Q-\Delta W That is, $\Delta U$ is independent of the path of the transformation, although $\Delta Q$ and $\Delta W$ are path dependent. In a reversible infinitesimal transformation, the infinitesimal changes $d Q$ and $d W$ are not exact differentials, in the sense that they do not represent the changes of definite functions, but their difference d U=d Q-d W is an exact differential.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
### 1.7 Magnetic Systems For a magnetic substance, the thermodynamic variables are the intensive magnetic field $H$, and the extensive magnetization $M$, which are unidirectional and uniform in space. The magnetic field is generated by external real currents (and not induced currents), and the magnet work done by the system is given by

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
d W=-H d M The first law takes the form d U=d Q-H d M which maps into that for a $P V T$ system under the correspondence $H \leftrightarrow-P, M \leftrightarrow V$. For a paramagnetic substance, a magnetic field induces a magnetization density given by \frac{M}{V}=\chi H The magnetic susceptibility $\chi$ obeys Curie's law \chi=\frac{c_{0}}{T}

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
Thus, we have the equation of state M=\frac{\kappa H}{T} where $\kappa=c_{0} V$. An idealized uniform ferromagnetic system has a phase transition at a critical temperature $T_{c}$, and becomes a permanent magnet for $T<T_{c}$ in the absence of external field. However, there is no phase transition in the presence of an external field.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
The equation of state is illustrated graphically in the $M T$ diagram of Figure 1.5. ![ This diagram depicts the temperature dependence of magnetization (M) in a ferromagnetic material, showing how magnetization decreases as temperature (T) approaches the critical temperature (Tc) for different values of the magnetic field (H), including zero and positive fields.](http://localhost:5001/subjects/065313dc-e010-4cf3-9daf-525801a906a2/images/204ead23-7ec3-4dd2-a9ff-40b5f38aa220/28642244-d175-43cc-88d7-d1a09b8e51d0-10_562_605_246_598.jpg) Figure 1.5 Equation of state of a uniform ferromagnet. A ferromagnetic transition occurs at a critical temperature at zero field. A real ferromagnet is not uniform, but made up of domains with different orientations of the magnetization. The configuration of the domains is such as to reduce the fringing fields that extend outside of the body, in order to minimize the magnetic energy. Each domain behaves according to the uniform case depicted in Figure 1.5. At a fixed $T<T_{c}$, the domain walls move in response to a change in $H$, to either consolidate old domains, or create new ones. This is a dissipative process, and leads to hysteresis, as shown in the $M H$ plot of Figure 1.6. At zero field, the magnetization is at either $a$ or $b$, depending on the history. This is the basis of magnetic memory.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
![ This diagram depicts a magnetic hysteresis loop showing the relationship between magnetization (M) and magnetic field strength (H), illustrating the lag of magnetization behind the applied magnetic field during magnetization and demagnetization cycles.](http://localhost:5001/subjects/065313dc-e010-4cf3-9daf-525801a906a2/images/204ead23-7ec3-4dd2-a9ff-40b5f38aa220/28642244-d175-43cc-88d7-d1a09b8e51d0-10_638_645_1792_576.jpg) Figure 1.6 Hysteresis in a ferromagnet is due to the formation of ferromagnetic domains.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
## Problems 1.1 Tenzing Norgay heated $1 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$ of water from 20 to $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, in order to take a bath before climbing Chomolungma. (a) How much energy did he use? Give the answer in kWh . (b) Show that the energy is enough to lift Tenzing's entire party of 14, of average weight 150 lb , from sea level to the top of Chomolungma (elev. $29,000 \mathrm{ft}$ ). 1.2 Referring to Figure 1.4, find the work done along the various paths on the closed cycle $a b, b c, c d, d e, e a$, and give the total work done in the closed cycle.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
How much heat is supplied to the system in one cycle? 1.3 An ideal gas undergoes a reversible transformation along the path \frac{V}{V_{0}}=\left(\frac{T}{T_{0}}\right)^{b} where $V_{0}, T_{0}$, and $b$ are constants. (a) Find the coefficient of thermal expansion. (b) Calculate the work done by the gas when the temperature increases by $\Delta T$. 1.4 In a nonuniform gas, the equation of state is valid locally, as long as the density does not change too rapidly with position. Consider a column of ideal gas under gravity at constant temperature. Find the density as a function of height, by balancing the forces acting on a volume element. 1.5 Two solid bodies labeled 1 and 2 are in thermal contact with each other.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
The initial temperatures were $T_{1}, T_{2}$, with $T_{1}>T_{2}$. The heat capacities are $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$, respectively. What is is final equilibrium temperature, if the bodies are completely isolated from the external world? 1.6 A paramagnetic substance is magnetized in an external magnetic field at constant temperature.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
How much work is require to attain a magnetization $M$ ? 1.7 A hysteresis curve (see Figure 1.6) is given by the formula M=M_{0} \tanh \left(H \pm H_{0}\right) where the + sign refers to the upper branch, and the - sign refers to the lower branch. The parameter $H_{0}$ is called the coercive force. Show that the work done by the system in one hysteresis cycle is $2 M_{0} H_{0}$. 1.8 The atomic nucleus The atomic nucleus contains typically fewer than 300 protons and neutrons.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
It is an example of a small system with both short- and long-range forces. The mass is given by the semi empirical Weizsäcker formula (See deShalit and Feshbach 1974): M=Z m_{p}+N m_{n}-a_{1} A+a_{2} A^{2 / 3}+a_{3} \frac{Z^{2}}{A^{1 / 3}}+a_{4} \frac{(Z-N)^{2}}{A}+\delta(A) where $Z$ is the number of protons, $N$ is the number of neutrons, and $A=Z+N$.

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
The masses of protons and neutrons are, respectively, $m_{p}, m_{n}$ and $a_{i}(i=1, \ldots, 4)$ are numerical constants. \text { Volume energy : } a_{1} & =16 \mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{c}^{2} \\ \text { Surface energy : } a_{2} & =19 \\ \text { Coulomb energy : } a_{3} & =0.72 \\ \text { Symmetry energy : } a_{4} & =28 The symmetry energy favors $N=Z$. The term $\delta(A)$ is the "pairing energy" that gives small fluctuations. Take $Z=N=A / 2, m_{n} \approx m_{p}$, and neglect $\delta(A)$, so that

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
M=\left(m_{p}-a_{1}\right) A+a_{2} A^{2 / 3}+\frac{a_{3}}{4} A^{5 / 3} Make a $\log$ plot of $M$ from $A=1$ to $A=10^{4}$, and indicate the range in which $M$ can be considered as extensive. 1.9 The false vacuum In the theory of the "inflationary universe," a pinpoint universe was created during the Big Bang in a "false" vacuum state characterized by a finite energy density $u_{0}$, while the true vacuum state should have zero energy density. (For a review see Guth, 1992).

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
An ordinary solid too has finite energy per unit volume; but it occupies a definite volume, given a total number of particles. If we put the solid in a box larger than that volume, it would not fill the box, but "rattle" in it. Not so the false vacuum. It must have the same energy density whatever its volume, and this makes it strange stuff indeed. (a) Imagine putting the false vacuum in a cylinder stopped with a piston, with the true vacuum outside. If we pull on the piston to increase the volume of the false vacuum by $d V$, show that the false vacuum performs work $d W=-u_{0} d V$. Hence the false vacuum has negative pressure $P=-u_{0}$. (b) According to general relativity, the radius $R$ of the universe obeys the equation \frac{d^{2} R}{d t^{2}}=-\frac{4 \pi}{3 c^{2}} G\left(u_{0}-3 P\right) R where $c$ is the velocity of light, and

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
G=6.673 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~cm}^{3} / \mathrm{g} \mathrm{~s}=6.707 \times 10^{-39} \mathrm{GeV}^{-2} \hbar c^{3} is Newton's constant (gravitational constant). For the false vacuum, this reduces to \frac{d^{2} R}{d t^{2}} & =\frac{R}{\tau^{2}} \\

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]
\tau & =\sqrt{\frac{3 c^{2}}{8 \pi G u_{0}}} Thus the radius of the universe expands exponentially with time constant $\tau$. According to theory, $u_{0}=\left(10^{15} \mathrm{GeV}\right)^{4} /(\hbar c)^{3}=10^{96} \mathrm{erg} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$. Show \tau \approx 10^{-34} s

[Document: Kapitel 1   Makroscopic View of Matter]

Zur Berechnung der Zustandssumme Z_{\mathrm{G}}=\operatorname{Sp}\left\{e^{-\beta(\hat{H}-\mu \hat{N})}\right\} verwenden wir die Fock-Basiszustände mit Eigenschaften: \hat{H}\left|\left\{n_{k}\right\}\right\rangle=\left(\sum_{k} E_{k} n_{k}\right)\left|\left\{n_{k}\right\}\right\rangle, \quad \hat{N}\left|\left\{n_{k}\right\}\right\rangle=\left(\sum_{k} n_{k}\right)\left|\left\{n_{k}\right\}\right\rangle

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
Damit erhalten wir: $\quad\left\langle\left\{n_{k}\right\}\right| e^{-\beta(\hat{H}-\mu \hat{N})}\left|\left\{n_{k}\right\}\right\rangle=e^{-\beta \sum_{k}\left(E_{k}-\mu\right) n_{k}}$ und: $\quad Z_{\mathrm{G}}=\sum_{n_{0}} \sum_{n_{1}} \ldots e^{-\beta \sum_{k}\left(E_{k}-\mu\right) n_{k}}=\prod_{k} \sum_{n_{k}}\left(e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}\right)^{n_{k}}$ - Bosonen: $n_{k}=0,1, \ldots, \infty$ \Rightarrow \quad Z_{\mathrm{G}}=\prod_{k} \sum_{n_{k}=0}^{\infty}\left(e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}\right)^{n_{k}}=\prod_{k} \frac{1}{1-e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}}

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
geometrische Reihe & \Rightarrow \quad J=-k_{B} T \ln Z_{\mathrm{G}}=k_{B} T \sum_{k} \ln \left(1-e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad\langle\hat{N}\rangle=-\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mu}=\sum_{k} \frac{e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}}{1-e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}}=\sum_{k} \underbrace{\frac{1}{e^{\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}-1}}_{\left\langle\hat{n}_{k}\right\rangle} - Fermionen: $\quad n_{k}=0,1$ & \Rightarrow \quad Z_{\mathrm{G}}=\prod_{k} \sum_{n_{k}=0,1}\left(e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}\right)^{n_{k}}=\prod_{k}\left(1+e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad J=-k_{B} T \ln Z_{\mathrm{G}}=-k_{B} T \sum_{k} \ln \left(1+e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad\langle\hat{N}\rangle=-\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mu}=\sum_{k} \frac{e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}}{1+e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}}=\sum_{k} \underbrace{\frac{1}{e^{\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}+1}}_{\left\langle\hat{n}_{k}\right\rangle} - Zum Vergleich: "klassische" ununterscheidbare Teilchen ("Boltzonen") & Z_{\mathrm{G}}=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty} Z_{\mathrm{K}}(N) e^{\beta \mu N}=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{N!}

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
\left(\sum_{k} e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}\right)^{N}=e^{\left(\sum_{k} e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}\right)} \\ & Z_{\mathrm{K}}(N)=\frac{1}{N!} \left(\sum_{k_{1}} e^{-\beta E_{k_{1}}}\right)\left(\sum_{k_{2}} e^{-\beta E_{k_{2}}}\right) \ldots\left(\sum_{k_{N}} e^{-\beta E_{k_{N}}}\right) Anzahl der möglichen Teilchenvertauschungen

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
Produkt der Zustandssummen der einzelnen Teilchen & \Rightarrow \quad J=-k_{B} T \ln Z_{\mathrm{G}}=\sum_{k} e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad\langle\hat{N}\rangle=-\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mu}=\sum_{k} \underbrace{e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}}_{=\left\langle\hat{n}_{k}\right\rangle} Zusammenfassung: mittlere Teilchenzahl im Zustand $\left|\phi_{k}\right\rangle$ -Bosonen:

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
\left\langle\hat{n}_{k}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{e^{\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}-1} "Bose-Einstein Verteilung" - Fermionen: \left\langle\hat{n}_{k}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{e^{\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}+1} "Fermi-Dirac Verteilung" -"klassische" Teilchen: \left\langle\hat{n}_{k}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{e^{\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}} "Maxwell-Boltzmann Verteilung"

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
### 5.1 Grundlagen: In diesem Kapitel betrachten wir ein ideales, d.h. nicht-wechselwirkendes Gas aus Fermionen mit Masse $m$ und Spin S in einem externen Potential $V_{\text {ex }}(\vec{r})$ (z.B. Box, harmonische Falle, ...).

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
Hamiltonoperator: $\quad \hat{H}=\sum_{i} \frac{\hat{\vec{p}}_{i}^{2}}{2 m}+V_{\text {ex }}\left(\hat{\vec{r}}_{i}\right)=\sum_{i} \hat{H}_{i}$ Weitere Annahme*: kein äußeres Magnetfeld. Dann besitzen alle Spinzustände die gleiche Energie und die Eigenwerte der EinteilchenSchrödingergleichung, \hat{H}_{i}\left|\phi_{k}^{(i)}, m_{s}\right\rangle=E_{k}\left|\phi_{k}^{(i)}, m_{s}\right\rangle \quad \quad m_{s}=-S,-S+1, \ldots, S sind jeweils $g_{S}=(2 S+1)$-fach entartet. ![

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
- Großkanon. Zustandssumme: $Z_{\mathrm{G}}=\prod_{k}\left(1+e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}\right)^{g_{S}}$ - Großkanon. Potential: $\quad J=-k_{B} T g_{S} \sum_{k} \ln \left(1+e^{-\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}\right)$ - Mittlere Teilchenzahl: $\quad N=\sum_{k} \frac{g_{S}}{e^{\beta\left(E_{k}-\mu\right)}+1}$

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
### 5.1.1 Zustandsdichte Im thermodynamischen Limes $N, V \rightarrow \infty$ geht der Abstand zwischen den Energieniveaus gegen Null und das Einteilchenspektrum wird kontinuierlich. In diesem Fall ist es sinnvoll die Zustandsdichte $D(E)$ einzuführen:

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
D(E)=\sum_{k, m_{s}} \delta\left(E-E_{k, m_{s}}\right)=g_{S} \sum_{k} \delta\left(E-E_{k}\right) Damit folgt für eine beliebige Funktion $F(E)$ der Energie: \sum_{k, m_{s}} F\left(E_{k, m_{s}}\right)=\int_{0}^{\infty} D(E) F(E) d E - Für große Systeme mit kleinem Abstand zwischen den Energieniveaus kann $D(E)$ durch eine kontinuierliche Funktion ersetzt werden.

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
![ This diagram depicts the Fermi-Dirac distribution function \( F(E) \) for electron energies \( E \) in a solid, showing the continuous probability distribution (blue curve) and the discrete energy levels \( E_k \) (red spikes) available to electrons.](http://localhost:5001/subjects/065313dc-e010-4cf3-9daf-525801a906a2/images/f03e3eba-4180-49e1-97b8-e2fe9e2a3eff/14cadde9-f499-439f-bb02-45c3799994d3-13_804_1438_1003_179.jpg) ![ This diagram depicts the Fermi-Dirac distribution function \( F(E) \) and the density of states \( D(E) \) as functions of energy \( E \), commonly used in solid-state physics to describe electron occupancy and available energy states in a material.](http://localhost:5001/subjects/065313dc-e010-4cf3-9daf-525801a906a2/images/f03e3eba-4180-49e1-97b8-e2fe9e2a3eff/14cadde9-f499-439f-bb02-45c3799994d3-13_667_1169_1003_1732.jpg) - Bedeutung der Zustandsdichte: D(E) d E=\text { Anzahl der Energieeigenzustände im Interval }[E, E+d E]

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
## Bsp1: Zustandsdichte für Gas in einer 3D Box: \left.\begin{array}{l} E_{\vec{k}}=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2 m}\left(k_{x}^{2}+k_{y}^{2}+k_{z}^{2}\right) \\ E_{\vec{n}}=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2 m}\left(\frac{2 \pi}{L}\right)^{2}\left(n_{x}^{2}+n_{y}^{2}+n_{z}^{2}\right) \end{array}\right\} \quad n_{i}=\frac{2 \pi}{L_{i}} n_{i}

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
periodische Randbedingungen ! \begin{array}{rlrl} \sum_{\vec{n}, m_{s}} F\left(E_{\vec{n}}\right) & =g_{S} \sum_{n_{x}, n_{y}, n_{z}} F\left(E_{\vec{n}}\right) \Delta n_{x} \Delta n_{y} \Delta n_{z} & & \left(\Delta n_{i}=1\right) \\ & =g_{S} \frac{L_{x} L_{y} L_{z}}{(2 \pi)^{3}} \sum_{k_{x}, k_{y}, k_{z}} F\left(E_{\vec{k}}\right) \Delta k_{x} \Delta k_{y} \Delta k_{z} & & \Delta k_{i}=\frac{2 \pi}{L_{i}} \rightarrow 0 \\ \left(L_{i} \rightarrow \infty\right) & =\frac{g_{S} V}{(2 \pi)^{3}} \int d^{3} k F\left(E_{\vec{k}}\right) & V=L_{x} L_{y} L_{z} \end{array} - Polarkoordinaten: $\int d^{3} k F\left(E_{|\vec{k}|}\right) \rightarrow 4 \pi \int_{0}^{\infty} k^{2} d k F\left(E_{k}\right)$ - Variablentransformation: \begin{gathered}

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 26.11]
E=\frac{\hbar^{2} k^{2}}{2 m} \Rightarrow \quad k=\sqrt{\frac{2 m E}{\hbar^{2}}} \quad d k=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\frac{2 m}{\hbar^{2}}} \frac{d E}{\sqrt{E}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \sum_{\vec{n}, m_{s}} F\left(E_{\vec{n}}\right)=\frac{g_{S} V}{4 \pi^{2}}\left(\frac{2 m}{\hbar^{2}}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \int_{0}^{\infty} d E \sqrt{E} F(E) \\ =\int_{0}^{\infty} d E D(E) F(E) \end{gathered} Zustandsdichte (Box, 3D): $\quad D(E)=\frac{g_{S} V}{4 \pi^{2}}\left(\frac{2 m}{\hbar^{2}}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \sqrt{E}$

### 7.4 Energie und Wärmekapazität von Phononen Mit der harmonischen Oszillator Näherung für Phononen, \hat{H}=\sum_{k} \hbar \omega_{k} \hat{a}_{k}^{\dagger} \hat{a}_{k} \quad k \equiv(\vec{k}, \lambda) erhält man direkt (analog zum Photonengas) die mittlere Energie U=\sum_{k} \frac{\hbar \omega_{k}}{e^{\beta \hbar \omega_{k}}-1} Thermodynamischer Limes: $\quad \Rightarrow U=V \int_{0}^{\infty} d \omega g(\omega) \frac{\hbar \omega}{e^{\beta \hbar \omega}-1}$ $g(\omega) \quad \ldots . \quad$ Zustandsdichte der Phononen (materialabhängig !) es gilt: $\quad V \int_{0}^{\infty} d \omega g(\omega)=3 N \quad=$ Anzahl der Schwingungsfreiheitsgrade (für 1 Atom/EZ)

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 16.12]
### 7.4.1 Einstein Modell Annahme: Alle Atome oszillieren mit gleicher Frequenz $\omega_{0}$ : g(\omega)=\frac{3 N}{V} \delta\left(\omega-\omega_{0}\right) - Energie: U=\frac{3 N \hbar \omega_{0}}{e^{\beta \hbar \omega_{0}}-1} \Rightarrow \begin{cases}3 N \hbar \omega_{0} e^{-\hbar \omega_{0} / k_{B} T} & k_{B} T<\hbar \omega_{0} \\ 3 N k_{B} T & k_{B} T>\hbar \omega_{0}\end{cases} - Wärmekapazität: \frac{C_{V}}{3 N k_{B}}=\frac{e^{\beta \hbar \omega_{0}}\left(\beta \hbar \omega_{0}\right)^{2}}{\left(e^{\beta \hbar \omega_{0}}-1\right)^{2}} \Rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{cc} \left(\frac{\hbar \omega_{0}}{k_{B} T}\right)^{2} e^{-\hbar \omega_{0} / k_{B} T} & k_{B} T<\hbar \omega_{0} \\ \sim 1 & k_{B} T>\hbar \omega_{0} \end{array}\right. ⇒ In diesem Modell sind für $k_{B} T<\hbar \omega_{0}$ alle Phononen "ausgefroren" (= exponentiell unterdrückt).

### 8.3 Das Van-der-Waals-Gas Aus der freien Energie für ein wechselwirkendes Gas (MF-Näherung), $$ F(T, N, V)=-k_{B} T N \ln \left(\frac{e(V-b N)}{N \lambda_{T}^{3}}\right)-\frac{a N^{2}}{V} $$ erhalten wir durch Ableitung ( $p=-\partial F /\left.\partial V\right|_{T, N}$ ) die Zustandsgleichung des Van-der-Waals-Gases in der üblichen Form: \left(p+\frac{a}{v^{2}}\right)(v-b)=k_{B} T \quad \text { mit } \quad v=\frac{V}{N} Bemerkung: Bis auf Korrekturen $\mathcal{O}\left(b^{2} / v^{2}\right)$ erhält man das gleiche Resultat auch aus der Virial- oder der Clusterentwicklung bis zur Ordnung $\mathrm{n}=2$. - Spezifische Wärme: $\quad C_{V}=-T \frac{\partial^{2} F}{\partial T^{2}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad C_{V}=\frac{3}{2} k_{B} N$ Gleich wie für das ideale Gas! ## 4. Quantenstatistik 4.1 Quantenmechanik (Wiederholung): - Ein quantenmechanisches System ist zu jedem Zeitpunkt durch eine Wellenfunktion $|\psi(t)\rangle$ in einem abstrakten Hilbertraum $\mathcal{H}$ beschrieben. - Die Zeitentwicklung ist durch die Schrödingergleichung bestimmt, $$

[Document: Folien Zur Vorlesung am 18.11]
\frac{d}{d t}|\psi(t)\rangle=-\frac{i}{\hbar} \hat{H}|\psi(t)\rangle \quad \Rightarrow \quad|\psi(t)\rangle=e^{-i \hat{H} t / \hbar}|\psi(0)\rangle $$ wobei der Hamiltonoperator $\hat{H}$ der Energie des Systems entspricht. - Der Hamiltonoperator ist "hermitesch" ( $\hat{H}^{\dagger}=\hat{H}$ ). Daraus folgt: \hat{H}\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle=E_{k}\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle \quad E_{k} \in \mathbb{R} und die Energieeigenzustände bilden eine vollständige Orthonormalbasis von $\mathcal{H}$ mit: \left\langle\varphi_{k} \mid \varphi_{k^{\prime}}\right\rangle=\delta_{k, k^{\prime}} \quad \sum_{k}\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle\left\langle\varphi_{k}\right|=\mathbb{1} - Alle observablen Größen werden durch hermitesche Operatoren $\hat{A}=\hat{A}^{\dagger}$ repräsentiert. Für ein System im Zustand $|\psi(t)\rangle$ ist der Erwartungswert von $\hat{A}$ gegeben durch

[Document: Folien Zur Vorlesung am 18.11]
\langle\hat{A}\rangle(t)=\langle\psi(t)| \hat{A}|\psi(t)\rangle - Sei $\hat{A}\left|a_{k}\right\rangle=a_{k}\left|a_{k}\right\rangle$, dann ist die Wahrscheinlichkeit bei einer einzelnen Messung den Wert $A=a_{k}$ zu erhalten gleich P\left(A=a_{k}\right)=\left|\left\langle a_{k} \mid \psi(t)\right\rangle\right|^{2} Wichtig: Selbst für ein vollständig bestimmtes System \hat{H},|\psi(0)\rangle \quad \Rightarrow \quad|\psi(t)\rangle=e^{-i \hat{H} t / \hbar}|\psi(0)\rangle (deterministisch) sind Messergebnisse in der Quantenmechanik i.A. zufällig verteilt.

[Document: Folien Zur Vorlesung am 18.11]
### 4.2 Der Dichteoperator Betrachten wir nun den Fall, dass der Anfangszustand nicht exakt bekannt ist, sondern nur, dass ein Zustand |\psi(t=0)\rangle=\left|\psi_{n}\right\rangle \quad \text { mit Wahrscheinlichkeit } \quad p_{n} \text { vorliegt.

[Document: Folien Zur Vorlesung am 18.11]
} Dann ist der verallgemeinerte Erwartungswert einer Observable: \langle\hat{A}\rangle(t)=\sum_{n} p_{n}\left\langle\psi_{n}(t)\right| \hat{A}\left|\psi_{n}(t)\right\rangle \quad \quad\left|\psi_{n}(t)\right\rangle=e^{-i \hat{H} t / \hbar}\left|\psi_{n}\right\rangle "Unbestimmtheit des Systems" \begin{aligned} &\langle\hat{A}\rangle(t)=\sum_{n} p_{n}\left\langle\psi_{n}(t)\right| \underbrace{\left(\sum_{k}\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle\left\langle\varphi_{k}\right|\right)}_{\mathbb{1}} \hat{A}\left|\psi_{n}(t)\right\rangle \\ &=\sum_{k}\left\langle\varphi_{k}\right| \hat{A} \underbrace{\sum_{n} p_{n}\left|\psi_{n}(t)\right\rangle\left\langle\psi_{n}(t)\right|}_{=: \hat{\rho}(t) \longrightarrow \text { Spur }})\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle=\operatorname{Spp} \hat{A} \hat{\rho}(t)\} \\ & \longrightarrow \text { "Dichteoperator" }

[Document: Folien Zur Vorlesung am 18.11]
\end{aligned} - Der Zustand eines nicht-vollständig bestimmten Quantensystems wird durch den Dichteoperator $\hat{\rho}(t)$ repräsentiert. - Mit Hilfe des Dichteoperators können Erwartungswerte von Observablen verallgemeinert als \langle\hat{A}\rangle(t)=\operatorname{Sp}\{\hat{A} \hat{\rho}(t)\} ausgedrückt werden.

[Document: Folien Zur Vorlesung am 18.11]
## Eigenschaften des Dichteoperators: - selbstadjungiert (="hermitesch"): $\quad \hat{\rho}^{\dagger}=\hat{\rho} \quad$ (folgt aus Definition) - Diagonalform: Da hermitesch, kann $\hat{\rho}$ immer in der Form \hat{\rho}=\sum_{k} p_{k}\left|\lambda_{k}\right\rangle\left\langle\lambda_{k}\right| geschrieben werden, wobei $\left|\lambda_{k}\right\rangle$ Eigenbasis von $\hat{\rho}$ und $p_{k} \in \mathbb{R}$ ist die Wahrscheinlichkeit, das System im Zustand $\left|\lambda_{k}\right\rangle$ zu finden. ## Ergänzung: Operatorwertige Funktionen In der Quantenstatistik verwenden wir wiederholt operatorwertige Funktionen, wie z.B. $\exp (-\beta \hat{H})$ oder $\ln (\hat{\rho})$. Diese Funktionen können formal über die Potenzreihenentwicklung der regulären Funktionen definiert werden und generell mit Hilfe der Eigenwertzerlegung berechnet werden.

[Document: Folien Zur Vorlesung am 18.11]
Sei $f(x \in R)$ eine analytische Funktion mit Potenzreihe: $f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_{n} x^{n}$ Dann definieren wir dazu die entsprechende operatorwertige Funktion als: f(\hat{A})=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_{n} \hat{A}^{n} Im relevanten Fall von hermetischen Operatoren können wir den Operator in seiner Eigenbasis darstellen \hat{A}=\sum_{k} \lambda_{k}\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle\left\langle\varphi_{k}\right| und da die $\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle$ eine Orthonormalbasis bilden gilt: \hat{A}^{n}=\left(\sum_{k_{1}} \lambda_{k_{1}}\left|\varphi_{k_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle\varphi_{k_{1}}\right|\right) \ldots\left(\sum_{k_{n}} \lambda_{k_{n}}\left|\varphi_{k_{n}}\right\rangle\left\langle\varphi_{k_{n}}\right|\right)=\sum_{k} \lambda_{k}^{n}\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle\left\langle\varphi_{k}\right| Damit kann die operatorwertige Funktion explizit berechnet werden, indem man $f(x)$ für jeden Eigenwert berechnet: f(\hat{A}) & =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_{n} \sum_{k} \lambda_{k}^{n}\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle\left\langle\varphi_{k}\right|=\sum_{k}\left(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_{n} \lambda_{k}^{n}\right)\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle\left\langle\varphi_{k}\right| \\ & =\sum_{k} f\left(\lambda_{k}\right)\left|\varphi_{k}\right\rangle\left\langle\varphi_{k}\right| Beispiel 1: In der statistischen Physik benötigen wir häufig die Exponentialfunktion des Hamiltonoperators, die wir einfach in der Energieeigenbasis auswerten können. e^{-\beta \hat{H}}=\sum_{k} e^{-\beta E_{k}}\left|E_{k}\right\rangle\left\langle E_{k}\right| Beispiel 2: Für die Berechnung der Entropie benötigen wir den Logarithmus des Dichteoperators. ### 11.2.3 Entwicklung der Entropie - Das H-Theorem Wir definieren eine Boltzmann-Entropie entsprechend S_{B}(t)=-k_{B} H(t):=\int d^{3} x s_{B}(\vec{x}, t) wobei $\quad s_{B}(\vec{x}, t)=-k_{B} \int d^{3} p f(\vec{x}, \vec{p}, t) \ln f(\vec{x}, \vec{p}, t)$ die lokale Entropiedichte bezeichnet.

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 27.01]
## "H-Theorem" i) Die gesamte (Boltzmann) Entropie des Systems kann nicht abnehmen \frac{d S_{B}(t)}{d t} \geq 0 ii) Die lokale Entropiedichte befolgt die Gleichung \frac{\partial s_{B}}{\partial t}+\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{j}_{s}=\left.\frac{\partial s_{B}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{Stoß}} \geq 0 mit Entropiestromdichte: \vec{j}_{s}(\vec{x}, t)=-\frac{k_{B}}{m} \int d^{3} p \vec{p} f(\vec{x}, \vec{p}, t) \ln f(\vec{x}, \vec{p}, t) - Die Entropie wächst monoton mit der Zeit → Irreversibilität! - Die Entropieerhöhung wird durch Stöße mit anderen Teilchen verursacht ("Molekulares Chaos")

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 27.01]

### 1.3.1 Wahrscheinlichkeiten Eine Größe (Zufallsvariable) $X$ kann zufällig einen der diskreten Werte $\left\{X_{n} \mid n=1, \ldots, N\right\}$ annehmen. Wir bezeichnen mit P\left(X_{n}\right) \equiv P\left(X=X_{n}\right) die Wahrscheinlichkeit, dass bei einem gegebenen Ereignis (z.B. in einem Experiment), der Wert $X=X_{n}$ auftritt. Das heisst, bei einer großen Anzahl von $M \rightarrow \infty$ Wiederholungen des selben Ereignisses wird der Fall $X=X_{n}$ insgesamt $N_{n}=P\left(X_{n}\right) \times M$ mal eintreten. | Es gilt: | $($ i) | $0 \leq P\left(X_{n}\right) \leq 1$ | positiv | | ---: | :--- | ---: | :--- |

### 1.3.2 Mittelwert, Varianz und Korrelationen - Der Mittelwert (oder Erwartungswert) einer Zufallsvariable, \langle X\rangle=\sum_{n} X_{n} P\left(X_{n}\right) \quad \text { bzw. } \quad\langle X\rangle=\int X p(X) d X bestimmt den Wert, der gemittelt über viele Ereignisse angenommen wird.

[Document: Folien zur VO am 14.10]
Achtung: Mittelwert $\neq$ wahrscheinlichster Wert! Analog dazu ist der Erwartungswert einer beliebigen Funktion $F(X)$ durch \langle F(X)\rangle=\sum_{n} F\left(X_{n}\right) P\left(X_{n}\right) \quad \text { bzw. } \quad\langle F(X)\rangle=\int F(X) p(X) d X gegeben.

[Document: Folien zur VO am 14.10]
- Die Varianz einer Verteilung, \left\langle\Delta X^{2}\right\rangle=\left\langle(X-\langle X\rangle)^{2}\right\rangle=\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle-\langle X\rangle^{2} bestimmt die mittlere Abweichung der tatsächlich auftretende Werte vom Mittelwert. D.h., nur wenn $\sqrt{\left\langle\Delta X^{2}\right\rangle} \lesssim\langle X\rangle$ ist der Mittelwert eine "brauchbare" Größe. Bsp:

## Mathematischer Einschub: "Eulersche Homogenitätsrelation" Sei $f\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{N}\right)$ eine homogene Funktion vom Grad $k$, d.h.: f\left(\lambda x_{1}, \ldots, \lambda x_{N}\right)=\lambda^{k} f\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{N}\right) Dann gilt: $\quad \sum_{i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}} x_{i}=k f\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{N}\right)$ Beweis: $\quad \Rightarrow$ Differenzieren von Gleichung $\left({ }^{*}\right)$ nach $\lambda$ :

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 22.10]
$\left.\begin{array}{lc} & \begin{array}{c}\text { Kettenregel } \\ \downarrow \\ \text { linke Seite: }\end{array} \\ & \frac{d}{d \lambda} f\left(\left\{\lambda x_{i}\right\}\right)=\sum_{i} \frac{\partial f\left(\left\{\lambda x_{i}\right\}\right)}{\partial\left(\lambda x_{i}\right)} x_{i} \\ \text { rechte Seite: } & \frac{d}{d \lambda}\left[\lambda^{k} f\left(\left\{x_{i}\right\}\right)\right]=k \lambda^{k-1} f\left(\left\{x_{i}\right\}\right)\end{array}\right\} \begin{aligned} & \text { setze } \\ & \lambda=1\end{aligned}$ Energie ist extensiv und daher: $\quad E(\lambda S, \lambda V, \lambda N)=\lambda E(S, V, N)$

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 22.10]
## "homogene Funktion 1. Grades" Aus Satz von Euler folgt: $\quad E(S, V, N)=\frac{\partial E}{\partial S} S+\frac{\partial E}{\partial V} V+\frac{\partial E}{\partial N} N$ oder: E=T S-p V+\mu N

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 22.10]

Potential: S \equiv S(E, V, N)=\frac{1}{T}(E+p V-\mu N) Aus d S=\frac{1}{T} d E+\frac{p}{T} d V-\frac{\mu}{T} d N ergeben sich die Relationen: \frac{1}{T}=\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial E}\right)_{V, N} \quad \frac{p}{T}=\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_{E, N} \quad-\frac{\mu}{T}=\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{E, V} Achtung: Im Gegensatz zu allen anderen therm. Potentialen hat $S$ nicht die Einheit einer Energie!

## Mathematischer Einschub: Legendre Transformation

Für eine Funktion $f(x)$ sei $p(x)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ die "konjugierte Variable" zu x.

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 22.10]
## gesucht: Eindeutige Funktion $g \equiv g(p)$ welche die selbe Information wie $f(x)$ enthält. Beispiel: $\quad f(x, y)=\frac{1}{2}(x-a y)^{2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad p(x)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=x-a y$ Versuch 1: $\quad g(p, y)=f(x(p), y)=\frac{p^{2}}{2}$ Problem: $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=-a(x-a y)=-a p \quad$ aber $\quad \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}=0$ Information über Abhängigkeit von weiteren Variablen und Parametern geht verloren, wenn p als unabhängige Variable aufgefasst wird. Versuch 2 (Legendre Transformation):

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 22.10]
\begin{aligned} & g(p, y)=f(x, y)-x p=-\frac{p^{2}}{2}-a p y \quad x \equiv x(p) \\ & \quad \Rightarrow \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}=-a p \end{aligned} Interpretation: aus Tangentengleichung: $g(p)=f(x)-p x$

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 22.10]

It illustrates how the tangent lines to \( f(x) \) relate to the values of the conjugate function \( g(p) \).](http://localhost:5001/subjects/065313dc-e010-4cf3-9daf-525801a906a2/images/9c30fad5-c8b6-433f-86a0-2f681028c6ad/4028e0a2-efec-4c96-959b-5032026f3a45-13_1206_1677_817_1249.jpg) eindeutige (injektive) Abbildung: $\{x, f(x)\} \rightarrow\{p, g(p)\}$

Gegeben: Funktion $f\left(x,\left\{y_{i}\right\}\right)$ und $p=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ sei die konjugierte Variable zu $x$. Def: "Legendre-transformierte Funktion" $\quad g\left(p,\left\{y_{i}\right\}\right)=f-p x$ - Differential: $d g=d(f-x p)=\underbrace{\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}}_{=p} d x+\sum_{i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y_{i}} d y_{i}-x d p-p d x$ =-x(p) d p+\sum_{i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y_{i}} d y_{i}=\frac{\partial g}{\partial p} d p+\sum_{i} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y_{i}} d y_{i} $\Rightarrow \mathrm{g}$ hängt von den unabhängigen Variablen $p$ und $\left\{y_{i}\right\} \mathrm{ab}$ ! - Wir erhalten $f(x)$ durch nochmalige Legendre Transformation von $g(p)$ : x=-\frac{\partial g}{\partial p} \quad g-p \frac{\partial g}{\partial p}=g+p x=f Bedingung: $p=f^{\prime}(x)$ muss invertierbar sein, d.h. $f^{\prime}(x)$ ist streng monoton wachsend oder fallend.

### 4.4 Extremaleigenschaften Zum Vergleich zweier Dichteoperatoren $\hat{\rho}$ und $\hat{\rho}^{\prime}$ betrachten wir die folgende Funktion: \mathbf{H}\left(\hat{\rho}, \hat{\rho}^{\prime}\right)=\operatorname{Sp}\left\{\hat{\rho}^{\prime}\left(\ln \hat{\rho}-\ln \hat{\rho}^{\prime}\right)\right\} \quad(\text { "Boltzmann'sche } \mathbf{H} \text {-Funktion")* } Für beliebige Dichteoperatoren mit $\operatorname{Sp}\{\hat{\rho}\}=\operatorname{Sp}\left\{\hat{\rho}^{\prime}\right\}=1$ gilt die Ungleichung: \mathbf{H}\left(\hat{\rho}, \hat{\rho}^{\prime}\right) \leq 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \operatorname{Sp}\left\{\hat{\rho}^{\prime} \ln \hat{\rho}^{\prime}\right\} \geq \operatorname{Sp}\left\{\hat{\rho}^{\prime} \ln \hat{\rho}\right\} Diese Ungleichung ist nützlich, um Extremaleigenschaften für die Gleichgewichtszustände \hat{\rho}=\hat{\rho}_{\mathrm{MK}}, \hat{\rho}_{\mathrm{K}}, \hat{\rho}_{\mathrm{G}}

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 25.11]
abzuleiten. *) H ....griechischer Großbuchstabe "Eta" Beweis von $\mathbf{H}\left(\hat{\rho}, \hat{\rho}^{\prime}\right) \leq 0$ : wir schreiben: $\quad \hat{\rho}=\sum_{k} p_{k}|k\rangle\langle k|, \quad \hat{\rho}^{\prime}=\sum_{n} p_{n}|n\rangle\langle n|$ dann: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{H}\left(\hat{\rho}, \hat{\rho}^{\prime}\right) & =\operatorname{Sp}\left\{\hat{\rho}^{\prime}\left(\ln \hat{\rho}-\ln \hat{\rho}^{\prime}\right)\right\}=\sum_{n} p_{n}\langle n|\left(\ln \hat{\rho}-\ln p_{n}\right)|n\rangle \\ & =\sum_{n} \sum_{k} p_{n}\langle n \mid k\rangle\langle k| \ln \frac{p_{k}}{p_{n}}|k\rangle\langle k \mid n\rangle

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 25.11]
\end{aligned} Es gilt die Ungleichung: \ln \frac{p_{k}}{p_{n}} & \leq \frac{p_{k}}{p_{n}}-1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{H}\left(\hat{\rho}, \hat{\rho}^{\prime}\right) & \leq \sum_{n} \sum_{k} p_{n}\langle n \mid k\rangle\langle k|\left(\frac{p_{k}}{p_{n}}-1\right)|k\rangle\langle k \mid n\rangle \\ & =\sum_{n} p_{n}\langle n|\left(\frac{\hat{\rho}}{p_{n}}-1\right)|n\rangle=\operatorname{Sp}\{\hat{\rho}\}-\operatorname{Sp}\left\{\hat{\rho}^{\prime}\right\}=0 ![

## Mathematischer Einschub: Vollständige und nicht vollständige Differentiale Sei $F(x, y)$ eine skalare Funktion zweier Variablen $x$ und $y$, dann ist d F=\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\right)_{y} d x+\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}\right)_{x} d y das vollständige (auch totale, oder exakte) Differential von $F$. \left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\right)_{y} \ldots \text { "partielle Ableitung" von } F \text { nach } x \text { bei konstantem } y " $d F$ ".... Änderung von $F \rightarrow F+d F$ bei infinitesimaler Änderung von x \rightarrow x+d x \text { und } y \rightarrow y+d y . \binom{\text { mathematisch präziser: }}{d F, d x, d y \text { sind linear Abbildungen ("1-Formen"), } \quad d F: \mathbb{R}^{2} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}} Es gilt: Gegeben ein vollständiges Differential

Speziell ist das Integral F\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)-F\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)=\int_{x_{0}, y_{0}}^{x_{1}, y_{1}} d F unabhängig vom $\boldsymbol{\operatorname { W e g }}\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right) \rightarrow\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$.

## vollständiges Differential ? Falls $d F$ vollständiges Differential, dann A(x, y)=\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\right)_{y} \quad B(x, y)=\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}\right)_{x} und wegen der Vertauschbarkeit der partiellen Ableitungen gilt: \left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial y}\right)_{x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=\left(\frac{\partial B}{\partial x}\right)_{y}

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 21.10]
## Allgemein: d F=\sum_{i=1}^{N} A_{i}\left(x_{1}, \ldots x_{N}\right) d x_{i} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{\partial A_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}=\frac{\partial A_{j}}{\partial x_{i}} \quad \forall x_{i} \neq x_{j} vollständiges Diff. | Konvention: | $d F$ | $\ldots$ | vollständiges Differential | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | |  | $\delta F$ | $\ldots$ | nicht vollständiges Differential |

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 21.10]
## Bedeutung für die Thermodynamik Sei $d F=\sum_{i=1}^{N} A_{i}\left(x_{1}, \ldots x_{N}\right) d x_{i}$ ein vollständiges Differential. Dann ist die Größe $F\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{N}\right)$ eine Zustandsfunktion, d.h. sie ist für jeden Gleichgewichtszustand eindeutig und unabhängig von der Vorgeschichte durch die Zustandsvariablen $x_{i}$ bestimmt. Bsp1: $\quad E \equiv E(V, T)=\frac{3}{2} N k_{B} T$

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 21.10]
d E=\underbrace{0}_{=A} \cdot d V+\underbrace{\frac{3}{2} N k_{B}}_{=B} \cdot d T \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial A}{\partial T}=0=\frac{\partial B}{\partial V} vollständiges Diff. ⇒ Energie ist Zustandsfunktion Bsp2: mechanische Arbeit (als Funktion von V und T ) \delta W=\underbrace{-p(T, V)}_{=A} \cdot d V+\underbrace{0}_{=B} \cdot d T \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\partial A}{\partial T}=-\frac{\partial p(T)}{\partial T} \neq 0=\frac{\partial B}{\partial V} kein vollständiges Diff. ⇒ Arbeit ist wegabhängig ! Daraus folgt auch das $\delta Q=d E-\delta W$ kein vollständiges Differential sein kann !

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 21.10]
## "Integrierender Faktor"

Für ein nicht-vollständiges Differential $\delta F$ kann immer eine Funktion $\lambda(x, y)$ gefunden werden, sodass

d F=\lambda(x, y) \delta F

ein vollständiges Differential ist.

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 21.10]
## Beispiel: \delta F=y d x-x d y \quad \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial y}\right)_{x}=1 \neq\left(\frac{\partial B}{\partial x}\right)_{y}=-1 (kein vollständiges Diff) Integrierender Faktor: $\quad \lambda(x, y)=\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ damit wird $d F=\lambda(x, y) \delta F=\frac{y}{x^{2}} d x-\frac{1}{x} d y$ zum vollständigen Diff.: \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial y}\right)_{x}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}=\left(\frac{\partial B}{\partial x}\right)_{y}

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 21.10]

Hauptsatz abstrakt-mathematisch formuliert und daraus die physikalischen Konsequenzen bezüglich des Transports von Wärme und der Unmöglichkeit eines Perpetuum mobiles 2. Art abgeleitet. - Historisch wurde der 2. Hauptsatz mit Hilfe dieser "physikalischen" Prinzipien formuliert: -"Kelvin'sche Aussage": Es gibt kein Perpetuum mobile zweiter Art.

Z.B., wäre es möglich ein PM 2. Art zu konstruieren, könnten wir damit periodisch Wärme von einem kalten in ein heißes Reservoir transferieren. - Es gibt noch weitere äquivalente Formulierungen des 2. ## Quantenmechanische Modellierung: Bei einem gegebenen, homogenen äußeren magnetischen Feld $\vec{B}$ wird die Energie der magnetischen Probe durch den Hamiltonoperator $$ \hat{H}=-\hat{\mathcal{M}} \cdot \vec{B}, \quad \text { mit } \quad \overrightarrow{\mathcal{M}}=\int_{V} \vec{M} d^{3} r=\sum_{i} \vec{\mu}_{i} $$

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 13.01]
beschrieben. Bei Kopplung des magnetischen Systems an ein Wärmebad ergibt sich daher die freie Energie F(T, \vec{B})=-k_{B} T \ln Z_{\mathrm{K}} mit der kanonischen Zustandssumme: $\quad Z_{\mathrm{K}}=\operatorname{Sp}\left\{e^{-\beta \hat{H}(\vec{B})}\right\}$ und den Ableitungen : $\quad S=-\left.\frac{\partial F}{\partial T}\right|_{\vec{B}}, \quad E=\langle\hat{H}\rangle=-\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln Z_{\mathrm{K}}$ Aus der Ableitung der freien Energie nach den Komponenten des Magnetfelds erhalten wir das magnetische Moment der gesamten Probe: \mathcal{M}_{k}=-\left.\frac{\partial F}{\partial B_{k}}\right|_{T}=\left.\frac{1}{\beta} \frac{\partial \ln Z_{\mathrm{K}}}{\partial B_{k}}\right|_{T}

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 13.01]
Weitere wichtige physikalische Größen erhält man aus den 2 . Ableitungen der freien Energie: - Spezifische Wärme (bei konstantem B-Feld): C_{B}=\left.\frac{\partial E}{\partial T}\right|_{\vec{B}}=\left.\frac{\partial E}{\partial S} \frac{\partial S}{\partial T}\right|_{\vec{B}}=-\left.T \frac{\partial^{2} F}{\partial T^{2}}\right|_{\vec{B}} - Magnetische Suszeptibilität (isotherm): \chi=\left.\frac{1}{V} \frac{\partial \mathcal{M}}{\partial B}\right|_{T}=-\left.\frac{1}{V} \frac{\partial^{2} F}{\partial B^{2}}\right|_{T} \quad(\overrightarrow{\mathcal{M}} \| \vec{B})

Sie entsprechen daher eigentlich der Enthalpie und der (Gibbs) freien Enthalpie aus der Thermodynamik: $E(S, \vec{B}) \quad \leftrightarrow \quad H(S, p, N)$

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 13.01]
$F(T, \vec{B}) \leftrightarrow G(T, p, N)$ *) Diese Beschreibung vernachlässigt die Energie des mag. Feldes selbst, sowie die externe elektrische Arbeit, welche zur Aufrechterhaltung des äußeren Felds verrichtet wird.

### 9.4 Das Ising Modell: Molekularfeldnäherung

Das Ising Modell ist in 1D und 2D exakt lösbar. Es ist aber instruktiv, zuerst eine Näherungslösung zu betrachten.

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 13.01]
### 9.4.1 Molekularfeld- ("mean-field") Näherung: Wir schreiben das Ising Modell als: H=\mu B \sum_{i} \sigma_{z}^{i}-J \sum_{\langle i, j\rangle} \sigma_{z}^{i} \sigma_{z}^{j}=\mu \sum_{i} \underbrace{\left(B-\frac{J}{\mu} \sum_{j}^{\mathrm{nn}} \sigma_{z}^{j}\right)}_{B_{\mathrm{eff}}} \sigma_{z}^{i} Die Austausch-WW der Nachbarspins wirkt sich wie ein zusätzliches lokales mag. Feld aus, dass jedoch von der Konfiguration der Spins abhängt.

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 13.01]
Näherung: $\quad B_{\text {eff }} \approx B-z \frac{J}{\mu}\left\langle\sigma_{z}\right\rangle$ z ... Anzahl der Nachbarspins - Das lokale Feld wird durch seinen Mittelwert approximiert. - Der Erwartungswert $\left\langle\sigma_{z}\right\rangle$ ist vorerst unbekannt, und muss am Ende der Rechnung selbstkonsistent bestimmt werden.

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 13.01]
## Molekularfeldnäherung (etwas genauer): Wir schreiben allgemein und noch ohne Näherung: \sigma_{z}^{i}=\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{i}\right\rangle+\left(\sigma_{z}^{i}-\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{i}\right\rangle\right)=\text { "Mittelwert" + "Fluktuationen" } Damit: \sigma_{z}^{i} \sigma_{z}^{j}= & {\left[\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{i}\right\rangle+\left(\sigma_{z}^{i}-\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{i}\right\rangle\right)\right]\left[\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{j}\right\rangle+\left(\sigma_{z}^{j}-\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{j}\right\rangle\right)\right] } \\ = & \left\langle\sigma_{z}^{i}\right\rangle\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{j}\right\rangle+\left(\sigma_{z}^{i}-\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{i}\right\rangle\right)\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{j}\right\rangle+\left(\sigma_{z}^{j}-\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{j}\right\rangle\right)\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{i}\right\rangle \\ & +(\underbrace{\left.\sigma_{z}^{i}-\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{i}\right\rangle\right)\left(\sigma_{z}^{j}-\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{j}\right\rangle\right)}_{\approx 0} \longleftarrow \begin{array}{c} \text { Kopplung zwischen } \\ \text { "Fluktuationen" } Molekularfeldnäherung: $\quad \sigma_{z}^{i} \sigma_{z}^{j} \rightarrow \sigma_{z}^{i}\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{j}\right\rangle+\sigma_{z}^{j}\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{i}\right\rangle-\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{i}\right\rangle\left\langle\sigma_{z}^{j}\right\rangle$ Der Beitrag der Fluktuationen der magnetischen Momente wird in der Wechselwirkung im Vergleich zu den mittleren Momenten vernachlässigt. Mit dieser Näherung reduziert sich das Ising Modell auf ein System von $N$ ungekoppelte Spins in einem (effektiven) Magnetfeld: \begin{gathered}

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 13.01]
H \rightarrow H_{\mathrm{MF}}=\mu B_{\mathrm{eff}} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sigma_{z}^{i}+\frac{z J}{2} N m^{2} \\ B_{\mathrm{eff}}=B+z \frac{J}{\mu} m, \quad \begin{array}{l} \text { "Energie-Offset" } \\ \text { (abhängig von m) }

[Document: Folien zur Vorlesung am 13.01]
\end{gathered} mag. Moment m \equiv-\left\langle\sigma_{z}\right\rangle effektives Magnetfeld Daher erhalten wir analog zu 9.2: $\quad Z_{\mathrm{MF}}=\left[2 e^{-\beta \frac{z J}{2} m^{2}} \cosh \left(\frac{\mu B_{\mathrm{eff}}}{k_{B} T}\right)\right]^{N}$ und aus $m=-\left.\frac{1}{\mu N \beta} \frac{\partial \ln Z_{\mathrm{MF}}}{\partial B_{\mathrm{eff}}}\right|_{T, m}$ folgt $\quad m=\tanh \left(\frac{\mu B+z J m}{k_{B} T}\right)$ Selbstkonsistenzgleichung für magnetisches Moment

### 2.5.1 Maxwell Relationen Zur Erinnerung: vollständiges Differential (Integrabilitätsbedingung) d F=\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\right)_{y} d x+\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}\right)_{x} d y \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}\right) ⇒ Angewandt auf thermodynamische Potentiale ergeben sich daraus die Maxwell Relationen für die Ableitungen von Zustandsgrößen. Bsp 1: $\quad d E(S, V, N)=T d S-p d V+\mu d N \quad$ (Energie)

[Document: Folien zur VO am 28.10]
\frac{\partial T}{\partial V}=\frac{\partial}{\partial V}\left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial S}\right)=\frac{\partial}{\partial S}\left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial V}\right)=-\frac{\partial p}{\partial S} \Rightarrow\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial V}\right)_{S, N}=-\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial S}\right)_{V, N} Bsp 2: $\quad d F(T, V, N)=-S d T-p d V+\mu d N \quad$ (Freie Energie) \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial V}=\frac{\partial}{\partial V}\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial N}\right)=\frac{\partial}{\partial N}\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\right)=-\frac{\partial p}{\partial N} \Rightarrow\left(\frac{\partial \mu}{\partial V}\right)_{T, N}=-\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial N}\right)_{T, V} ⇒ Für einkomponentiges Gas: insgesamt 12 verschiedene Relationen! Gedächtnishilfe: "Maxwell-Diagramm"/ "Guggenheim Quadrat"

## Eigenschaften der Jacobi-Determinante - ungerade bezüglich Vertauschung: $\frac{\partial(f, g)}{\partial(u, v)}=-\frac{\partial(g, f)}{\partial(u, v)}=-\frac{\partial(f, g)}{\partial(v, u)}$ - verallgemeinerte Kettenregel: $\quad \frac{\partial(f, g)}{\partial(x, y)}=\frac{\partial(f, g)}{\partial(u, v)} \cdot \frac{\partial(u, v)}{\partial(x, y)}$ - Rücktransformation: $\quad \frac{\partial(u, v)}{\partial(x, y)}=\left(\frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(u, v)}\right)^{-1}$ - Spezialfall partielle Ableitung: $\left.\quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\right|_{v}=\frac{\partial(f, v)}{\partial(u, v)}$

I: Man versucht aus mikrokospischen Zuständen, also Zuständen im Phasenraum, makroskopische Zustände herzuleiten mit Hilfe von Wahrscheinlichkeiten und gemittelten Ergebnissen. I: Da gibt es einmal das mikrokanonische Ensemble mit den Variablen $E, V$ und $N$, bei dem wir ein abgeschlossenes System, also ein System ohne Teilchen- und Energieaustausch, betrachten. Dann gibt es das kanonische Ensemble, dass sich mit den Variablen T, V, N beschrieben lässt, bei dem wir ein geschlossenes System betrachten, also keinen Teilchenaustausch, jedoch Energieaustausch zulassen. Des Weiteren gibt es noch das großkanonische Ensemble, hier betrachten wir ein offenes System mit Teilchen- und Energieaustausch. Man kann es mit den Variablen $T, V$ und $\mu$ beschrieben. P: Wie komme ich den auf die Energie eines solchen Systems? I: Das kann man sich über die Zustandssumme herleiten? P: Wie sehen denn die Zustandssummen für die verschiedenen Systeme aus? I: (Ich schreibe alle Zustandssummen für die verschiedenen Ensembles hin) Mikrokanonisch:

[Document: Altklausuren]

## Alim 2 P: Ich möchte die Prüfung gleichmäßig auf die 3 Schwerpunkte Statistische Mechanik, Thermodynamik und Quantenstatistik aufteilen. Wir beginnen mit statistischer Mechanik. Wann benutzt man die statistische Mechanik (oder so ähnlich)? I: Wir betrachten makroskopische Systeme mit großer Teilchenanzahl und Volumen, als den thermodynamischen Limes. Es ist in diesem Fall nicht mehr möglich die Bewegungsgleichung zu lösen, außerdem hängen diese empfindlich von den Anfangsbedingungen ab. Für Messgrößen betrachten wir den zeitlichen Mittelwert dieser, da sich der Mikrozustand ständig ändert. Statt dem Zeitmittelwert können wir aufgrund der Ergondenhypothese ebenso den Ensemblemittelwert betrachten, wobei das Ensemble die Gesamtheit der Mikrozustände ist, die mit einem Makrozustand verträglich sind. Jedem Mikrozusand kann eine Wahrscheinlichkeit zugeordnet werden.

[Document: Altklausuren]

I: We use statistical mechanics to describe systems with large number of particles $N$, since it is impossible to solve the equations of motion for all particles. $P$ : What do we assume when applying statistical mechanics? ## Preface The main purpose of statistical physics is to clarify the properties of matter in aggregate, in terms of the physical laws governing atomic motion. The present book is a textbook for advanced undergraduates.

[Document: Huang]
It assumes background knowledge of classical and quantum physics, on an introductory undergraduate level. In introducing the properties of matter, one faces a dilemma: should one follow thermodynamics, and bring in entropy as that mystical object sooming out of the second law, or should one first discuss the randomness of atomic collisions? I choose thermodynamics, because it describes everyday experience.

[Document: Huang]
(And it is profound, as one realizes after having absorbed the atomic view.) This book may be divided into three parts, the classical view, the quantum view, and advanced applications. The classical portion occupies first thirteen chapters, more than half the book. It covers the classical ensembles of statistical mechanics and stochastic processes. The latter subject includes Brownian motion, probability theory, and the Fokker-Planck and Langevin equations, with emphasis on physical understanding. To illustrate the use of statistical methods beyond the theory of matter, there are brief discussions of entropy in information theory, Brownian motion in the stock market, and the Monte Carlo method in computer simulations. The quantum part comprises five chapters. On quantum ensembles, the discussion emphasizes what makes quantum mechanics different from classical mechanics-the quantum phase. Applications include Fermi statistics and semiconductors, and Bose statistics and Bose-Einstein condensation. The final three chapters deal with advanced topics. A long chapter introduces what might be viewed as a major phenomenology after thermodynamics-the GinsburgLandau theory of the order parameter. The last two chapters are devoted to the special kind of quantum order as manifested in superfluidity and superconductivity. The present edition is expanded from an earlier edition, which was based on a one-semester course given at MIT. I am grateful for the opportunity to interact with students who took the course, known in MIT (ingo as 8.08, and people who helped me teach the course: Alexander Lomakin, Patrick Lee, and Lisa Randall. Kerson Huang 2009 "

[Document: Huang]
### 1.1 Viewing the World at Different Scales The world puts on different faces for observers using different scales in the measurement of space and time. The everyday, macroscopic world, as perceived on the scale of meters and seconds, looks very different from that of the atomic, microscopic world, which is seen on scales smaller by some ten orders of magnitude. Different still is the submicroscopic ealm of quarks, which is revealed only when the scale shrinks further by another ten orders of magnitude. With an expanding scale in the opposite direction, one enters the regime of astronomy, and ultimately cosmology. These different pictures arise from different ways of organizing data, while the basic laws of physics remain the same. The physical laws at the smallest accessible length scale are the most "fundamental," but they are of little use on a larger scale, where we must deal with different physical variables. A complete knowledge of quarks tells us nothing about the structure of nuclei, unless we can define nuclear variables in terms of quarks, and obtain their equations of motion from those for quarks. Needless to say, we are unable to do this in detail, although we can see how this could be done in principle.

[Document: Huang]
Therefore, each regime of scales has to be described phenomenologically, in terms of variables and laws observable in that regime. For example, an atom is described in terms of electrons and nuclei without reference to quarks. The subnuclear world enters the equations only implicitly, through such parameters as the mass ratio of electron to proton, which we take from experiments in the atomic regime. Similarly, in the macroscopic domain, where atoms are too small to be visible, we describe matter in terms of phenomenological variables such as pressure and temperature.

The atomic structure of matter enters the picture implicitly, in terms of properties such as density and heat capacity, which can be measured by macroscopic instruments. This book is concerned mainly with statistical methods, which provide a bridge between the microscopic and the macroscopic world.
